name: Building Web APIs with Python
author: Recurse
subject: web
description: FastAPI (with Flask comparisons): routes, Pydantic validation, errors, dependencies, SQLAlchemy, auth, tests and deploys.

lesson.intro: Most Python developer jobs involve building or maintaining a web API. This pack walks through building one with FastAPI, the most popular modern choice, with Flask comparisons along the way: routing and parameters, validation with Pydantic, errors and status codes, dependency injection, a SQLAlchemy database layer, authentication, testing with pytest, async endpoints and background work, and running it in production.
objectives: Build FastAPI endpoints with path, query and JSON body parameters validated by Pydantic models
Return correct status codes and consistent error bodies, mapping domain errors in one place
Use dependencies for database sessions and authentication, and store data with SQLAlchemy
Test an API's contract with pytest, TestClient and dependency overrides
Choose between def and async def endpoints and run an API in production with workers and migrations

sections.title: From an HTTP request to a Python function
sections.body:
A phone app sends `POST /orders` with a JSON body and an Authorization header. Somewhere a Python function must receive that order, check it, save it and answer `201 Created` with JSON. A **web framework** is the code in between, so you can write the function and nothing else.

Quick HTTP recap (How the Web Works and REST APIs in Practice go deeper): a request has a **method**, a **path** with an optional query string, **headers** and an optional **body**. A response has a **status code**, headers and a body, usually JSON for an API.

What every web framework does for you:
- **Routing**: maps a method and path such as `GET /books/42` to one of your functions.
- **Parsing**: turns path segments, query strings, headers and JSON bodies into Python values.
- **Validation**: rejects bad input with a 4xx response before your code runs.
- **Serialization**: converts your return value to JSON with the right status code and headers.
- **Errors**: turns exceptions into proper HTTP error responses.

A server process sits in front: it accepts connections, speaks HTTP and calls the framework. Python has two interfaces for this. **WSGI** is the classic synchronous one (Flask, Django), served by gunicorn. **ASGI** is its async successor (FastAPI, which is built on Starlette), served by **uvicorn**, and it also supports websockets.

The three frameworks you will see in job postings:
- **FastAPI**: type hints drive everything. Parameters are parsed and validated from their annotations, Pydantic models describe JSON bodies, and interactive OpenAPI docs appear at `/docs` for free. This pack uses it as the main example.
- **Flask**: small and explicit, with a huge ecosystem of extensions; you read the request yourself and choose your own libraries.
- **Django**: batteries included (ORM, admin site, auth, migrations), with Django REST Framework for APIs.

The decorator in `@app.get("/health")` is the registration pattern from Advanced Python: it records your function in the app's routing table and returns it unchanged.
sections.code:
# main.py: FastAPI                     run: uvicorn main:app --reload
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/health")
def health() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"status": "ok"}            # a returned dict becomes a JSON response


# app.py: Flask                        run: flask --app app run --debug
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}            # Flask also turns a dict into JSON


# $ curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# content-type: application/json
#
# {"status":"ok"}
sections.pitfall: Running the development server in production. --reload and Flask's debug mode watch files and can expose an interactive debugger; production uses a proper server setup, covered in the last section.

activity.title: Build a tiny router
activity.prompt: This is what a framework's routing table does. In handle(), look up routes.get((method, path)). If it is missing, return 405 when some route has the same path (any(p == path for _, p in routes)), otherwise 404. Call the handler with body only for POST.

props.task: Print 200 {'status': 'ok'}, then 201 {'msg': 'hi'}, then 404 {'detail': 'Not Found'}, then 405 {'detail': 'Method Not Allowed'}.

check.question: Which interface and server pair does a FastAPI app use?
check.explanation: FastAPI is built on Starlette, an ASGI framework, and uvicorn is the usual ASGI server. Flask and Django are WSGI frameworks served by gunicorn or similar.

sections.title: Routes, path parameters and query parameters
sections.body:
`GET /books/42` and `GET /books?q=dune&limit=5` carry inputs in two different places, and choosing the right one is part of API design. A **path parameter** identifies one resource: the book with id 42. **Query parameters** modify a request for a collection: filter, search, sort, paginate.

In FastAPI the function signature declares both:
- A name in braces in the path, `/books/{book_id}`, matched by a parameter `book_id: int`, is a path parameter. FastAPI converts the text to an int and answers **422 Unprocessable Entity** with a JSON description if it cannot, so your function never sees `"abc"`.
- Any other simple parameter is a query parameter. A default value makes it optional (`q: str | None = None`), and no default makes it required.
- `Query(10, ge=1, le=100)` (or `Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10`) adds validation, so `?limit=0` is rejected and `?limit=1000000` cannot dump the whole table.

Routes are matched **in the order they are declared**. If `/users/{user_id}` comes before `/users/me`, a request for `/users/me` matches the first route with user_id = "me" and fails validation or, worse, does the wrong thing. Declare fixed paths before parameterized ones.

Flask does the same with converters in the path, `@app.get("/books/<int:book_id>")`, where a non-matching segment gives 404 rather than 422, and with `request.args.get("q")` for query strings, which you convert and validate yourself (or with an extension).

REST APIs in Practice covers the design side: plural nouns for collections, ids in the path, filters and pagination in the query string, and never a verb such as `/getBook` in the URL.
sections.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Query

app = FastAPI()
BOOKS = {1: {"id": 1, "title": "Dune", "year": 1965},
         2: {"id": 2, "title": "Emma", "year": 1815}}

@app.get("/books/{book_id}")
def get_book(book_id: int):                       # path parameter, converted to int
    if book_id not in BOOKS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Book not found")
    return BOOKS[book_id]

@app.get("/books")
def list_books(q: str | None = None,              # optional query parameter: ?q=du
               limit: int = Query(10, ge=1, le=100)):    # default 10, must be 1 to 100
    found = [b for b in BOOKS.values() if q is None or q.lower() in b["title"].lower()]
    return found[:limit]


from fastapi.testclient import TestClient     # sends requests without a server
client = TestClient(app)

print(client.get("/books/1").json())          # {'id': 1, 'title': 'Dune', 'year': 1965}
print(client.get("/books/abc").status_code)   # 422: "abc" is not an integer
print(client.get("/books?q=EM").json())       # [{'id': 2, 'title': 'Emma', 'year': 1815}]
print(client.get("/books?limit=0").status_code)   # 422: limit must be >= 1
print(client.get("/books/99").json())         # {'detail': 'Book not found'}

# Flask equivalent:
# @app.get("/books/<int:book_id>")            # "abc" does not match: 404, not 422
# def get_book(book_id): ...
# q = request.args.get("q")                   # you parse and validate yourself
sections.pitfall: Declaring /users/{user_id} before /users/me. The first matching route wins, so "me" is treated as a user id; put fixed paths first.

activity.title: Match paths like a framework
activity.prompt: Use `re.sub(r"\{(\w+)\}", r"(?P<\1>[^/]+)", pattern)` inside compile_route, so each {name} becomes a named group. Then try swapping the first two routes and watch /users/me turn into user_id 'me'.

check.question: A FastAPI route is declared as @app.get("/books/{book_id}") with book_id: int. What does GET /books/abc return?
choices: 422 with a JSON error saying book_id must be an integer
check.explanation: FastAPI validates the path parameter against its type before calling your function and returns 422 with details. A Flask <int:book_id> route would not match at all, giving 404.

sections.title: Request bodies and validation with Pydantic
sections.body:
Every field a client sends is untrusted: missing, the wrong type, too long, negative, or crafted to break something. Checking all of that by hand in every endpoint is tedious and easy to get wrong. FastAPI hands the job to **Pydantic**: you describe the data once as a class, and it parses, converts and validates.

A **Pydantic model** subclasses `BaseModel` and declares fields with type hints. When an endpoint parameter is a model, FastAPI reads the JSON body into it:
- Types are enforced, with sensible conversion by default: the string "1965" becomes the int 1965, but "soon" is an error.
- `Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)` and `Field(ge=1450)` add constraints. `EmailStr`, `HttpUrl` and `datetime` handle common formats (EmailStr needs the email-validator extra).
- `@field_validator` runs custom checks or clean-ups, such as trimming and lowercasing tags.
- Nested models and `list[Model]` validate whole JSON documents.

If anything fails, FastAPI answers **422** with a list of every problem, each with a location (`["body", "title"]`), a type code and a message, before your function runs. Clients can show each error next to the right form field.

Use **separate models for input and output**. `BookIn` is what clients may send; `BookOut` adds the server-generated id. For users this matters even more: `UserCreate` has a password, `UserOut` must never include the password hash. Setting `response_model=UserOut` (or the return type) makes FastAPI filter the response to exactly those fields, so a stray attribute cannot leak.

`model.model_dump()` converts a model to a dict and `Model.model_validate(data)` builds one from a dict, which is also how you validate data from files, queues or other APIs, not just HTTP.

In Flask you call the validation yourself: `BookIn.model_validate(request.get_json())` inside try/except `ValidationError`, or use an extension that wires it up.
sections.code:
from datetime import date

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator

app = FastAPI()
BOOKS: dict[int, dict] = {}

class BookIn(BaseModel):                      # what clients may send
    title: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)
    author: str
    year: int = Field(ge=1450, le=date.today().year)
    tags: list[str] = []                      # safe: Pydantic copies defaults

    @field_validator("tags")
    @classmethod
    def clean_tags(cls, tags: list[str]) -> list[str]:
        return [t.strip().lower() for t in tags]

class BookOut(BookIn):                        # what the API returns
    id: int

@app.post("/books", status_code=201, response_model=BookOut)
def create_book(book: BookIn):                # a model parameter is the JSON body
    new = BookOut(id=len(BOOKS) + 1, **book.model_dump())
    BOOKS[new.id] = new.model_dump()
    return new


from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
client = TestClient(app)

r = client.post("/books", json={"title": "Dune", "author": "Herbert",
                                "year": "1965", "tags": [" SciFi "]})
print(r.status_code, r.json())
# 201 {'title': 'Dune', 'author': 'Herbert', 'year': 1965, 'tags': ['scifi'], 'id': 1}

r = client.post("/books", json={"title": "", "year": "soon"})
print(r.status_code, [(e["loc"], e["type"]) for e in r.json()["detail"]])
# 422 [(['body', 'title'], 'string_too_short'), (['body', 'author'], 'missing'),
#      (['body', 'year'], 'int_parsing')]
sections.pitfall: Returning the database object or a dict straight from an endpoint without a response model. Every field goes out, including ones like password_hash or internal flags; declare an output model.

activity.title: Validate like Pydantic, by hand
activity.prompt: Collect every problem instead of stopping at the first. Read fields with data.get(), convert year with int() inside try/except, check the ranges, and return (None, errors) if the list is not empty.

props.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Book:
    title: str
    year: int

def validate_book(data):
    """Return (Book, []) for valid data, or (None, errors) listing EVERY problem."""
    errors = []
    # title: required ("title: required"), a non-empty string ("title: must not be empty")
    # year: required ("year: required"), an int or digit string ("year: not an integer"),
    #       from 1450 to 2100 ("year: out of range")
    return Book(data.get("title"), data.get("year")), errors

for data in [{"title": "Dune", "year": "1965"}, {"title": "", "year": 3000}, {"year": "soon"}]:
    print(validate_book(data))
props.task: Print (Book(title='Dune', year=1965), []), then (None, ['title: must not be empty', 'year: out of range']), then (None, ['title: required', 'year: not an integer']).
props.expectOutput:
(Book(title='Dune', year=1965), [])
(None, ['title: must not be empty', 'year: out of range'])
(None, ['title: required', 'year: not an integer'])

check.question: A client POSTs {"title": "", "year": "soon"} to the create_book endpoint above. What happens?
choices: The book is saved with an empty title
FastAPI returns 500 because the year cannot be converted
Only the first error is returned
FastAPI returns 422 listing every problem, and create_book never runs
check.explanation: Pydantic validates the whole body and reports all errors together: title too short, author missing and year not an integer. Your function is called only with valid data.

sections.title: Status codes, errors and consistent responses
sections.body:
A mobile developer calls your API, gets `200 OK` with `{"error": "not found"}`, and their app shows an empty screen instead of a "not found" message, because their HTTP client only checks the status code. Status codes are part of your API's contract, so pick them deliberately.

The ones a CRUD API uses daily:
- **200** OK with a body; **201** Created after a POST that made something (set `status_code=201` on the route); **204** No Content after a successful DELETE.
- **400** for a malformed request, **422** for well-formed JSON that breaks validation (FastAPI's default).
- **401** when the caller is not authenticated (missing or invalid credentials); **403** when they are authenticated but not allowed.
- **404** when the resource does not exist, or when you do not want to reveal that it exists to this user.
- **409** Conflict for a duplicate email or a state clash, **429** Too Many Requests when rate limited.
- **500** only ever means "our bug". Never return it on purpose for a client mistake.

In a FastAPI route, `raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Book not found")` stops the handler and sends `{"detail": "Book not found"}` with that status. FastAPI uses the `detail` key for its own errors too, so following the same shape keeps every error consistent for clients.

Keep HTTP out of your business logic. Code that checks stock or charges cards should raise **domain exceptions** (`OutOfStock`, `PaymentDeclined`) that know nothing about HTTP. One `@app.exception_handler` maps each to a status code and body. The domain code stays testable without a web server, and the mapping lives in one place instead of try/except blocks in every route.

Any exception you do not handle becomes a 500 with a generic body, and the traceback goes to your logs, not to the client. Leaking stack traces, SQL or file paths in responses hands attackers a map of your system.

Flask's equivalents are `abort(404)` and `@app.errorhandler(OutOfStock)`, with `jsonify` or a returned dict for the body.
sections.pitfall: Returning 200 with {"error": ...} in the body. Clients, monitoring and caches all read the status code; use a 4xx or 5xx so failures look like failures.

activity.title: Trigger each error on purpose
activity.prompt: This mock API stores tasks. Send requests that produce 400, 404, 405 and 415 responses and read each error body. The codes mean the same in every API, including the ones you build with FastAPI.

check.question: A logged-in user requests DELETE /teams/7, but they are not a member of team 7. Which status fits best?
choices: 403 Forbidden (or 404 if you hide that the team exists)
check.explanation: The user is authenticated, so 401 is wrong; they are simply not allowed. Many APIs return 404 instead so outsiders cannot even confirm the team exists.

sections.title: Dependency injection with Depends
sections.body:
Almost every endpoint needs the same few things: a database session, the current user, the settings, maybe pagination parameters. Creating them inside each function repeats code and makes testing hard, because the test cannot swap in a fake. FastAPI's answer is **dependency injection**: an endpoint declares what it needs, and the framework provides it.

A **dependency** is any function (or class). Declaring a parameter as `Annotated[Database, Depends(get_db)]` tells FastAPI to call `get_db` for each request and pass in the result. Dependencies can have their own parameters, including headers, query parameters and other dependencies, so they form a graph that FastAPI resolves per request. Within one request each dependency runs once, even if several others ask for it.

Three patterns cover most real use:
- **Resources with cleanup**: a dependency that `yield`s, like `get_db`. Code before the yield opens a session, code after it closes the session (and can roll back on error) once the response is done. It is the context manager idea, wired into the request.
- **Authentication**: `get_current_user` reads a header or token, raises 401 if it is missing or invalid, and returns the user. Any endpoint that lists it is protected, and the check cannot be forgotten inside the function body.
- **Shared parameters**: pagination (`page`, `size`) or filters declared once and reused across list endpoints.

`Annotated` aliases such as `CurrentUser = Annotated[str, Depends(get_current_user)]` keep signatures short and consistent across a codebase.

The testing payoff: `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: fake_db` replaces a dependency everywhere for the duration of a test, without patching imports. That is the same principle as Design Patterns' dependency injection, applied by the framework.

Flask has no built-in equivalent. Apps store per-request objects on `flask.g`, open and close sessions in `before_request` and `teardown_appcontext` hooks, and protect routes with decorators such as `@login_required` from Flask-Login.
sections.pitfall: Creating a database connection at import time and sharing it across all requests. Concurrent requests then interleave transactions on one connection; use a pool, and hand out a session per request through a yield dependency.

check.question: What runs the code after the yield in a dependency such as get_db?
choices: The client, when it closes the connection
Nothing: code after yield is ignored
FastAPI, after the response has been produced, even if the endpoint raised
check.explanation: FastAPI treats a yield dependency like a context manager: setup before the yield, cleanup after the request is handled. Wrapping the yield in try/finally guarantees the cleanup on errors too.

sections.title: A database layer with SQLAlchemy
sections.body:
Your API's data has to outlive the process, so it goes in a database: SQLite while learning, PostgreSQL in most production Python shops. Python code talks to it in one of two ways, and job postings expect at least a working knowledge of both.

**Raw SQL with a driver**: `sqlite3` (standard library) or `psycopg` for PostgreSQL. You write the SQL and always pass values as **parameters** (`WHERE title = ?` with a tuple of values), never with f-strings, which is how SQL injection happens. Simple, explicit and fast, but you map rows to objects yourself.

**An ORM** (object-relational mapper) maps tables to classes and rows to objects. **SQLAlchemy** is the standard in the Python world outside Django (which has its own ORM). In its 2.0 style:
- Models subclass a `DeclarativeBase`, with columns declared as `Mapped[int] = mapped_column(...)` and links between tables as `relationship()`.
- An **engine** holds the connection pool for one database URL, which comes from configuration (an environment variable), not the code.
- A **Session** is a unit of work: you `add` objects, query with `select(...)`, and `commit()` writes everything in one transaction (or `rollback()` undoes it).
- In a web app you create **one session per request**, through a yield dependency, and close it afterwards.

Schema changes go through **migrations**, not `create_all`: **Alembic** compares your models with the database, generates a migration script (`alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add isbn"`) that you review and commit, and applies it with `alembic upgrade head` during deployment.

ORMs make one performance trap easy: **lazy loading**. Looping over 100 books and touching `book.author` can fire 100 extra queries, the N+1 problem from Databases in Practice. Load related rows up front with `select(Book).options(selectinload(Book.author))`, and watch the generated SQL (`create_engine(..., echo=True)`) while developing.

You will also meet **SQLModel**, which merges SQLAlchemy models and Pydantic models into one class, and async engines (`create_async_engine` with asyncpg) for async endpoints.
sections.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, String, create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column, relationship

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class Author(Base):
    __tablename__ = "authors"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100), unique=True)
    books: Mapped[list["Book"]] = relationship(back_populates="author")

class Book(Base):
    __tablename__ = "books"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    author_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("authors.id"))
    author: Mapped[Author] = relationship(back_populates="books")

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///:memory:")  # e.g. postgresql+psycopg://... in production
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)              # real projects use Alembic migrations

with Session(engine) as session:              # in an API: one session per request
    herbert = Author(name="Frank Herbert")
    session.add_all([Book(title="Dune", author=herbert),
                     Book(title="Dune Messiah", author=herbert)])
    session.commit()

    stmt = (select(Book).join(Book.author)
            .where(Author.name == "Frank Herbert").order_by(Book.title))
    for book in session.scalars(stmt):
        print(book.id, book.title, "by", book.author.name)
# 1 Dune by Frank Herbert
# 2 Dune Messiah by Frank Herbert

# The same lookup with the standard library's sqlite3, parameters always bound:
# conn.execute("SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE title = ?", (title,))
sections.pitfall: Building SQL with f-strings, even inside an ORM's text() call. Bind every value as a parameter; the driver then sends it as data, so it can never become part of the SQL.

check.question: Why does a web app usually create one SQLAlchemy Session per request instead of one for the whole app?
choices: Sessions can only run one query each
Each request gets its own unit of work and transaction, so concurrent requests cannot mix their changes
A global session is slower to import
check.explanation: A Session tracks pending changes and an open transaction. Sharing one between concurrent requests interleaves their work; a session per request, closed afterwards, keeps them isolated while the engine's pool reuses connections.

sections.title: Authentication and authorization basics
sections.body:
Two questions guard every write endpoint. **Authentication**: who is calling? **Authorization**: is this caller allowed to do this to this particular resource? Getting the first wrong lets strangers in; getting the second wrong lets one customer read another customer's orders, which is the most common serious API vulnerability (OWASP calls it broken object level authorization).

**Passwords** are never stored, only slow, salted hashes of them. Use a library built for it, such as argon2 (argon2-cffi or pwdlib) or bcrypt; the standard library's `hashlib.scrypt` in the example is also a proper slow hash. Compare secrets with `hmac.compare_digest`, which takes the same time whether the first or the last character differs. Rate-limit the login endpoint, and give the same error for a wrong username and a wrong password.

After login, the client gets a **token** and sends it on every request in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. Two common kinds:
- **Opaque session tokens**: a random string (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`) that the server looks up in a database or cache. Easy to revoke: delete the row.
- **Signed tokens (JWTs)**: the token itself carries claims such as the user id (`sub`), role and expiry (`exp`), signed with a server secret. Any server can verify one without a lookup, but a JWT stays valid until it expires, so keep lifetimes short and pair them with refresh tokens. The signature only stops tampering: the payload is merely base64-encoded, so never put secrets in it.

In FastAPI, `OAuth2PasswordBearer` reads the bearer token, `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` parses a login form (it needs the python-multipart package), and a `current_user` dependency turns the token into a user or raises **401**. Authorization checks then raise **403**: by role (admins only) and, crucially, by ownership: load the order, and if `order.user_id != user.id`, refuse. Checking only that someone is logged in is not authorization.

Browser apps often use **cookie sessions** instead of bearer tokens, which brings CSRF protection into play (Secure Coding for the Web). Larger systems delegate login to an identity provider with OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.
sections.pitfall: Checking that a user is logged in but not that they own the resource. GET /orders/1043 must verify order.user_id matches the caller, or any user can read any order by changing the number.

activity.title: Verify a signed token
activity.prompt: This is how a JWT's signature works, with the standard library. In verify(), recompute the HMAC of body exactly as sign() does, return None unless hmac.compare_digest(expected, sig) is true, then decode the payload and return None if it has expired.

props.task: Print {'sub': 'ana', 'role': 'member', 'exp': 1000}, then None for the forged token, then None for the expired one.

check.question: Bo is logged in and calls GET /orders/77, which belongs to Ana. The endpoint only checks that a valid token was sent. What is this bug called?
check.explanation: Authentication worked, but nobody checked that order 77 belongs to Bo. Every endpoint that loads a resource by id must compare its owner with the current user (or return 404).

sections.title: Testing an API with pytest and TestClient
sections.code:
# tests/test_books.py
import pytest
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from books_api import BookRepo, app, get_current_user, get_repo


@pytest.fixture
def client():
    repo = BookRepo()                                    # fresh, empty store per test
    app.dependency_overrides[get_repo] = lambda: repo
    app.dependency_overrides[get_current_user] = lambda: "test-user"
    with TestClient(app) as c:
        yield c
    app.dependency_overrides.clear()                     # don't leak into other tests


def test_create_then_fetch(client):
    r = client.post("/books", json={"title": "Dune", "year": 1965})
    assert r.status_code == 201
    book_id = r.json()["id"]
    assert client.get(f"/books/{book_id}").json() == {"id": book_id, "title": "Dune", "year": 1965}


def test_missing_book_is_404(client):
    r = client.get("/books/999")
    assert r.status_code == 404
    assert r.json() == {"detail": "Book not found"}


@pytest.mark.parametrize("payload", [{}, {"title": "", "year": 1965}, {"title": "X", "year": "soon"}])
def test_invalid_payloads_are_rejected(client, payload):
    assert client.post("/books", json=payload).status_code == 422


def test_writes_need_a_token(client):
    del app.dependency_overrides[get_current_user]       # use the real check
    r = client.post("/books", json={"title": "Dune", "year": 1965})
    assert r.status_code == 401

$ pytest -q tests/test_books.py
......                                                      [100%]
6 passed in 0.05s
sections.pitfall: Checking only the status code. A 200 with the wrong body, a missing field or another user's data still passes; assert on the JSON your clients depend on.

check.question: Why does the client fixture call app.dependency_overrides.clear() after its yield?
choices: So overrides from one test cannot leak into later tests that expect the real dependencies
To make the tests run faster
check.explanation: dependency_overrides lives on the shared app object. Without cleanup, a test that relies on the real auth check could silently run with the fake user from an earlier test.

sections.title: Sync or async endpoints, and background work
sections.body:
FastAPI accepts both `def` and `async def` endpoints, and choosing wrong is one of the most common performance bugs in FastAPI apps. The rule follows from how each kind runs.

- A plain `def` endpoint runs in a **thread pool**. Blocking calls inside it, such as `requests.get`, `time.sleep`, the `sqlite3` or `psycopg` drivers, or a synchronous SQLAlchemy session, tie up one pool thread while other requests carry on in other threads. This is the safe default.
- An `async def` endpoint runs directly on the **event loop**. Every await (an `httpx.AsyncClient` request, an async database driver such as asyncpg, `asyncio.sleep`) lets the loop serve other requests meanwhile, so one worker can juggle thousands of slow network calls. But a single blocking call inside it, a `time.sleep`, a `requests.get` or a heavy computation, freezes **every** request on that worker until it returns.

So: use `async def` only when everything slow inside it is awaited with an async library. If you are calling blocking libraries, use plain `def`, or move the blocking part into a thread with `await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...)`. Dependencies follow the same rule.

**Work the client should not wait for.** Sending a welcome email or resizing an uploaded image should not delay the response:
- `BackgroundTasks` runs a function after the response is sent, in the same process. Fine for small jobs, but the work is lost if the process restarts.
- Anything slow, important or retryable goes to a **task queue**: the endpoint puts a job on a broker (Redis, RabbitMQ) and returns 202 Accepted, and separate worker processes (Celery, RQ, Dramatiq, arq) run it with retries. This is the queue-and-workers pattern from system design.
- CPU-heavy work (reports, image processing, machine learning inference) belongs in workers or separate services, never in the event loop.

Flask is synchronous: each request occupies a worker thread or process, which suits blocking libraries. Flask can run `async def` views, but each request still holds its worker, so it does not bring FastAPI-style concurrency (Quart is the async variant of Flask).
sections.pitfall: Calling a blocking library inside async def. requests.get or time.sleep in an async endpoint stalls every request on the worker; use an async client, plain def, or asyncio.to_thread.

check.question: An endpoint calls requests.get(url, timeout=10) (a blocking library). How should it be declared?
choices: It cannot be used in FastAPI at all
async def, so it is faster
Plain def, so FastAPI runs it in a thread pool
async def with time.sleep(0) before the call
check.explanation: Blocking code belongs in a plain def endpoint, which FastAPI runs in a worker thread. In an async def endpoint it would block the event loop for up to 10 seconds.

sections.title: Running and deploying a Python API
sections.body:
`uvicorn main:app --reload` is perfect on your laptop: it restarts on every save and listens only on localhost. Production needs a few changes, and interviewers like to ask what they are.

**Processes.** One Python process uses one CPU core for Python code. Production runs several **worker processes**: `uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4`, or FastAPI's own CLI, `fastapi run main.py --workers 4`. A common starting point is about one worker per core, then measure. Each worker has its own memory, so module-level caches are per worker, not shared. On Kubernetes or a container platform, teams often run one worker per container and let the platform run more containers. Flask and Django run under a WSGI server such as gunicorn, for example `gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 "app:create_app()"`.

**In front of the app**, a reverse proxy or the platform's load balancer terminates HTTPS, spreads traffic across instances and handles slow clients. uvicorn trusts the proxy's X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto headers only from addresses listed in `--forwarded-allow-ips` (localhost by default), so set it to your proxy's address and the app sees the real client address and scheme.

**Configuration and data.** Settings and secrets come from environment variables (Python Tooling covers the pattern). Database migrations (`alembic upgrade head`) run as a release step before the new code receives traffic, and migrations should stay compatible with the old code still running during a rolling deploy.

**Observability.** Log to stdout in a structured format and let the platform collect it. Add a cheap `GET /health` endpoint for load balancers and orchestrators, and track request rates, error rates and latency.

**Packaging.** A Docker image makes the app run the same everywhere (Docker Basics covers images and layers): a slim Python base, dependencies installed in their own layer before the code is copied so rebuilds are fast, and a non-root user.

**Where it runs**: a platform as a service (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku) for side projects; container services (Google Cloud Run, AWS App Runner or ECS, Azure Container Apps) or Kubernetes at work. Shipping Code: CI/CD and the Cloud covers the pipelines that build the image, run the tests and deploy on merge.

Finally, decide whether `/docs` should be public. It documents every endpoint, which is great for partners and unwanted for an internal admin API.
sections.code:
# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt   # cached unless requirements change
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser                                         # never run as root
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "2"]

# Development: auto-reload, localhost only
$ uvicorn app.main:app --reload
# Production without Docker: several workers on all interfaces
$ uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4
# Flask (WSGI) equivalent
$ gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 "app:create_app()"
# Release step, before new code takes traffic
$ alembic upgrade head
sections.pitfall: Keeping per-user state in a module-level dict or the local disk. With several workers and instances, the next request may land on a different process; store sessions, caches and uploads in a database, Redis or object storage.

check.question: An API runs with --workers 4. A module-level dict caches recent results. What is true?
choices: Each worker process has its own copy, so the cache is not shared and can disagree between requests
Only the first worker can write to it
All four workers share the dict
check.explanation: Workers are separate processes with separate memory. Shared state belongs in an external store such as Redis or the database.

keyTerms.definition: The asynchronous interface between Python web servers and frameworks, used by FastAPI and Starlette and served by uvicorn.
The classic synchronous interface between Python web servers and frameworks, used by Flask and Django and served by gunicorn.
A value taken from a URL segment, such as 42 in /books/42, usually identifying one resource.
A key=value pair after ? in a URL, used to filter, search, sort or paginate a collection.
A class subclassing BaseModel whose type hints and Field constraints parse and validate data, such as a JSON body.
The status FastAPI returns when a request is well-formed but fails validation, listing every error.
A FastAPI route setting that filters and validates the response against a model, so extra fields cannot leak.
Declaring what an endpoint needs with Depends, so the framework provides it per request and tests can override it.
An object-relational mapper, such as SQLAlchemy, that maps database tables to classes and rows to objects.
A unit of work that tracks loaded and new objects and commits or rolls back their changes in one transaction.
A versioned script, such as one generated by Alembic, that changes a database schema in a repeatable way.
A credential sent in the Authorization: Bearer header that proves who the caller is.
A JSON Web Token: base64-encoded claims plus a signature, verifiable without a database lookup but readable by anyone.
FastAPI's in-process client that sends requests through the whole app in tests without starting a server.
A broker plus worker processes (Celery, RQ) that run slow or retryable jobs outside the request.
One of several copies of the app run by the server to use multiple CPU cores; each has its own memory.

summary: A framework routes requests to functions and handles parsing, validation, serialization and errors; FastAPI uses ASGI and uvicorn, Flask uses WSGI.
Path parameters identify resources, query parameters filter collections, and Pydantic models validate JSON bodies with 422 on failure.
Pick status codes deliberately, keep one error shape, and map domain exceptions to HTTP in one place.
Depends supplies sessions, users and settings per request, and dependency_overrides makes them easy to fake in tests.
SQLAlchemy sessions are per request, values are always bound as parameters, and Alembic migrations change the schema.
Hash passwords slowly, verify tokens, and check ownership on every resource, not just login.
Use def for blocking code and async def only with async libraries; queue heavy work; run several workers behind a proxy in production.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who knows basic Python what happens, step by step, between a phone app sending POST /books with a JSON body and FastAPI sending back 201 Created, including where validation, dependencies and the database come in.

questions.question: Which job is NOT something a web framework like FastAPI or Flask does for you?
choices: Turning an HTTPException into a 404 response
Converting a returned dict into a JSON response
Deciding which business rules an order must satisfy
questions.explanation: Routing, parsing, serialization and error responses are framework plumbing. The business rules are your code, which is why keeping them in plain functions makes them easy to test.

questions.question: Match each framework or server with its description.

pairs.right: ASGI framework where type hints drive parsing, validation and docs
Small, explicit WSGI framework with many extensions
Batteries-included framework with ORM, admin and auth
ASGI server that runs FastAPI apps
Process-managing WSGI server often used for Flask and Django

questions.explanation: Frameworks shape how you write handlers; servers accept connections and call the framework. FastAPI plus uvicorn and Flask plus gunicorn are the common pairs.

questions.question: What path does FastAPI serve its interactive, auto-generated API documentation on by default?
questions.explanation: FastAPI builds an OpenAPI schema from your routes and models (at /openapi.json) and serves Swagger UI at /docs and ReDoc at /redoc.

questions.question: Complete the decorator so this function handles DELETE requests to /books/{book_id}.
questions.explanation: FastAPI (and Flask 2.0 and later) has one decorator per HTTP method: get, post, put, patch and delete. A DELETE request to a path registered only with get would receive 405 Method Not Allowed.

questions.question: You need an endpoint that searches books by title and returns at most 20 results. How should the inputs arrive?
choices: GET /books with the search term in a header
questions.explanation: Search terms, filters and page sizes modify a request for the books collection, so they belong in the query string. Path segments identify specific resources.

questions.question: Complete the signature so page is an optional query parameter that defaults to 1 and must be at least 1.
questions.explanation: Query declares a query-string parameter with a default and constraints, so ?page=0 is rejected with 422. Path is for path segments and Body for JSON bodies.

questions.question: GET /users/me returns 422: user_id should be a valid integer. Why?
choices: me is a reserved word in FastAPI
Routes match in declaration order, so /users/me hits /users/{user_id} first; declare /users/me before it
FastAPI does not allow two routes under /users
questions.explanation: The parameterized route was declared first and matches any single segment, including "me", which then fails int conversion. Fixed paths must come before parameterized ones.

questions.question: In FastAPI, def list_books(q: str | None = None, limit: int = 10). Which request is rejected?
questions.explanation: limit is declared as an int, and "five" cannot be converted, so FastAPI answers 422. Both parameters have defaults, so leaving either out is fine.

questions.question: Why have both a UserCreate and a UserOut model instead of one User model?
choices: It makes responses faster to serialize
Pydantic cannot reuse a model twice
Input needs fields such as password that must never be returned, and output has server fields such as id
FastAPI requires every endpoint to have two models
questions.explanation: Separate models make the contract explicit in both directions. response_model=UserOut filters the response, so a password hash can never slip out even if the object you return has one.

questions.question: What status code does FastAPI return when a request body fails Pydantic validation?
questions.explanation: 422 Unprocessable Entity: the JSON parsed fine, but its content broke the rules. The body lists each error with its location, type and message.

questions.question: With year: int in a Pydantic model (default settings), which JSON values for year are accepted? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: By default Pydantic converts a numeric string such as "1965" to an int. A float with a fractional part, text and null are rejected for a required int. Strict mode would also reject the string.

questions.question: Complete the model so name must be between 2 and 50 characters long.
questions.explanation: Field adds constraints to a model field; for strings they are min_length and max_length. Query is for query parameters, not body fields.

questions.question: Match each situation with the status code an API should return.

pairs.left: Signup with an email that is already registered
Request without any credentials to a protected endpoint
An unhandled exception in your code

questions.explanation: The status code is the first thing clients and monitoring read. 409 signals a conflict with existing state, and 500 should only ever appear for your own bugs.

questions.question: Why raise a domain exception such as OutOfStock in business code and map it with @app.exception_handler, instead of raising HTTPException there?
choices: FastAPI forbids HTTPException outside route functions
Business code stays free of HTTP, so it can be reused and tested without a web framework, and the mapping lives in one place
questions.explanation: The same stock logic might run from a CLI, a queue worker or a test. HTTPException belongs at the web edge; domain errors are translated to HTTP there, once.

questions.question: Clients report that failed lookups look like successes in their dashboards. What is wrong?
choices: It returns 200 for a missing book; raise HTTPException(status_code=404, ...) instead
The function should return a string
The error message should be in a header
questions.explanation: Returning a dict always produces 200, so every client and monitoring tool counts the failure as a success. HTTPException sends a 404 with the detail message.

questions.question: Why should an API never include a stack trace in an error response?
questions.answer: Stack traces reveal file paths, library versions, SQL and code structure that help attackers. Log the trace on the server and return a generic message with a status code.
questions.explanation: Debug pages and verbose errors are a classic source of information disclosure. A request id in the response lets support find the full trace in the logs.

questions.question: How do you make a test use a fake user instead of the real get_current_user dependency?
choices: Delete the dependency from the endpoint during tests
Edit the endpoint to accept a test flag
questions.explanation: dependency_overrides maps the original dependency to a replacement for every endpoint that uses it. Clear it after the test (a fixture can do this) so tests do not leak into each other.

questions.question: Complete the dependency so the session is always closed after the request.
questions.explanation: yield hands the session to the endpoint and pauses; FastAPI resumes the function after the response, so finally runs the close. With return, the finally block would close the session before the endpoint used it.

questions.question: Which are good jobs for a FastAPI dependency? Select all that apply.
choices: Providing a database session per request
Authenticating the caller and returning the current user
Holding the business rules for calculating an invoice total
Loading application settings once and sharing them
questions.explanation: Dependencies supply what endpoints need: resources, identity, parameters, configuration. Business rules belong in plain functions or services that endpoints call, so they stay testable on their own.

questions.question: Two dependencies used by the same endpoint both declare Depends(get_db). During one request, how many times does get_db run?
choices: It raises an error for the duplicate
Once: FastAPI caches a dependency's result within a request
questions.explanation: By default FastAPI reuses a dependency's value within one request, so both see the same session and the same transaction. Depends(get_db, use_cache=False) would force a separate call.

questions.question: Looping over 50 books and printing book.author.name runs 51 SQL queries. What fixes it?
choices: Load authors with the books, for example select(Book).options(selectinload(Book.author))
questions.explanation: Each first access to book.author lazily loads it with its own query. selectinload (or joinedload) fetches all the authors in one extra query up front, turning 51 queries into 2.

questions.question: Put the steps for changing a production database schema with Alembic in order.
items: Generate a migration with alembic revision --autogenerate
Review and edit the generated script
Commit it with the code change
Run alembic upgrade head during deployment
questions.explanation: Autogenerate is a draft, not a guarantee (it can miss renames, for example), so a human reviews it. The migration ships with the code and runs as part of the release.

questions.question: This lookup is vulnerable. What is the problem?
choices: The query should use LIKE instead of =
The f-string puts user input into the SQL text, allowing SQL injection; pass it as a parameter
questions.explanation: A title such as x' OR '1'='1 changes the query's logic. conn.execute("... WHERE title = ?", (title,)) sends the value separately, so it is always treated as data.

questions.question: Apply all pending Alembic migrations to the database.
questions.explanation: head is the newest revision. Deployment pipelines run this before (or as) the new code starts, so the schema matches what the code expects.

questions.question: Which is the right way to store user passwords?
choices: With a slow, salted password hash such as argon2, bcrypt or scrypt
In plain text in a separate table
Encrypted with AES so they can be recovered
questions.explanation: Slow, salted hashes make stolen databases expensive to crack, and the salt defeats precomputed tables. Fast hashes like plain SHA-256 can be guessed billions of times per second, and anything reversible can be reversed by whoever steals the key.

questions.question: Which statements about JWT access tokens are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Anyone holding the token can read its payload, because it is only base64-encoded
The signature stops a client from changing the claims undetected
A JWT can be revoked instantly by deleting it on the server
Short expiry times limit the damage of a stolen token
It is safe to put the user's password in the payload because it is signed
questions.explanation: Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality. Because servers verify JWTs without a lookup, there is nothing to delete; revocation needs short lifetimes, refresh tokens or a deny list.

questions.question: A request arrives with a valid token, but the user's role is not allowed to delete books. Which HTTP status code should the API return?
questions.explanation: 401 means not authenticated (no or bad credentials). This caller is known, just not permitted, so 403 Forbidden.

questions.question: Why compare tokens and password hashes with hmac.compare_digest instead of ==?
questions.answer: == stops at the first different character, so response times leak how much of a guess was right. compare_digest takes the same time regardless, preventing timing attacks.
questions.explanation: Timing differences are tiny but measurable over many requests. Security-sensitive comparisons of secrets should always be constant-time.

questions.question: What does FastAPI's TestClient do when a test calls client.get("/books/1")?
choices: Reads the response from a recorded cassette file
Opens a real network connection to a running server
Runs the request through the app in-process (routing, validation, dependencies) and returns the response
questions.explanation: TestClient talks to the ASGI app directly, so tests exercise the full request handling without starting uvicorn or touching the network.

questions.question: Which checks belong in the test suite for a POST /orders endpoint? Select all that apply.
choices: A valid order returns 201 and the created order in the body
A payload with a negative quantity returns 422
A request without a token returns 401
One user cannot read another user's order
The framework's router matches URLs correctly
questions.explanation: Test your contract and your rules: success, validation, authentication and authorization. The framework's own routing is already tested by its maintainers.
questions.concept: what to test in an API

questions.question: test_admin_only passes when run alone but fails when run after test_member_view. What is the likely cause?
choices: The override set in test_member_view is never removed, so the second test runs with a fake member user
questions.explanation: dependency_overrides is global to the app. Setting it inside a test without restoring it leaks state; do it in a fixture that clears the overrides after the yield, or use monkeypatch-style cleanup.

questions.question: Four requests hit an async def endpoint that calls time.sleep(1) at the same moment, on one worker. Roughly how long until the last response?
questions.explanation: time.sleep blocks the event loop, so the requests are handled one after another. With await asyncio.sleep(1), or a plain def endpoint in the thread pool, they would overlap and finish in about 1 second.

questions.question: Which tasks should go to a task queue with workers rather than run inside the request? Select all that apply.
choices: Sending a batch of 5,000 notification emails
Reading one row by primary key
questions.explanation: Slow or heavy work moves to workers so responses stay fast and the job can be retried. Quick lookups and validation are part of answering the request.

questions.question: What is the trade-off of FastAPI's BackgroundTasks compared with a task queue such as Celery or RQ?
questions.answer: BackgroundTasks is simple and needs no extra infrastructure, but runs in the web process after the response and is lost if the process dies, with no retries. A queue persists jobs and runs them in separate workers with retries and scaling.
questions.explanation: Use BackgroundTasks for small best-effort work. Anything that must happen, takes long, or needs retries belongs on a queue.

questions.question: Which change belongs in production but not on your laptop?
choices: Running several worker processes behind a load balancer that terminates HTTPS
Printing every SQL statement with echo=True
questions.explanation: --reload, echo=True and localhost-only binding are development conveniences. Production runs multiple workers on all interfaces behind a proxy or load balancer that handles TLS.

questions.question: Put the steps of a typical deploy of a new API version in order.
items: CI runs the tests on the merged commit
Build and push the Docker image
Roll out the new containers gradually
Watch health checks, error rates and latency
questions.explanation: Tests gate the build, migrations prepare the schema before new code depends on it, and a gradual rollout with monitoring lets you roll back before every user is affected.

questions.question: Why does the Dockerfile copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying the rest of the code?
choices: pip cannot see the code otherwise
Docker caches that layer, so code-only changes rebuild in seconds instead of reinstalling every package
requirements.txt must be the first file in any image
questions.explanation: Each instruction is a cached layer, rebuilt only when its inputs change. Dependencies change rarely and code changes often, so installing dependencies first keeps rebuilds fast.

questions.question: Start the FastAPI app object app in app/main.py with uvicorn, listening on all interfaces on port 8000, with 4 worker processes.
questions.explanation: app.main:app is module path, colon, variable name. --host 0.0.0.0 accepts connections from outside the container or machine, and --workers starts several processes to use more CPU cores.
